newsitem.title: USA: HBO makes strong showing at Emmys.
newsitem.headline: HBO makes strong showing at Emmys.

text.p: People who do not get cable are missing out on some of the best TV available, if the Emmy Award voters are to be trusted.
Cable programmes beat out network programmes in several awards at the Primetime Emmys Sunday night, with Home Box Office (HBO) making an especially strong showing.
Taking a total of 14 Emmys, HBO came in second only to NBC, which won 20. By comparison, the much larger ABC won 12 awards and CBS took 11.

Because Emmy winners are decided by a relatively small group of industry peers, they are seen as a measure of quality rather than popularity. HBO, which has only been eligible for Emmys since 1988, has made a consistently strong showing since then. In 1993 it was the top award winner.
But more striking than the number of wins this year was the high praise HBO and several other cable stations received at the awards podium and backstage.

"I think the best movies being made today are on HBO, Showtime and Turner," (Turner Network Television), said longtime director John Frankenheimer, who won an award for the TNT miniseries "Andersonville."
"The material on these stations is far superior to what's being made for feature films," Franhenheimer added.
"Thanks to HBO for continuing to make movies that are about something," said Paula Weinstein, one of the team of writers on the HBO movie, "Truman," which also won an Emmy.

But the praise did not come solely from those associated with cable stations. Several actors and others involved with network shows conceded that when their TV set at home is on, it is most likely tuned to a cable channel.

Along with "Truman", HBO won Emmys for best supporting actor in a comedy series, with "The Larry Sanders Show" star Rip Torn beating out others from the NBC hits "Frasier" and "Seinfeld." The cable programmer, which reaches a comparatively small 23 million U.S. households, also won for best variety series ("Dennis Miller Live") and best actor in a miniseries or special (Alan Rickman in "Rasputin").
Other cable stations, including TNT, which took three awards, as well as Showtme, A&E and American Movie Classics, which took two apiece, also helped to chip away at the networks' dominance.
